V02-E-001: Each generation seems to need new polite words for things that make people uncomfortable, and each new word eventually acquires the sting of the one it replaced. A term coined to soften the description of a disability or a humble occupation begins neutral, but because it is used to refer to the same people, held in the same regard, it gradually absorbs the attitudes attached to them. Within a few decades the once-gentle term is heard as an insult, and reformers propose another. This cycle does not show that changing words is pointless; a fresh term can briefly signal respect and break a habit of mockery. It does show that vocabulary cannot carry the burden of changing attitudes on its own, since words take their colouring from the attitudes they name rather than the other way round.
V02-E-002: Newspapers often print an error on the front page and the correction, days later, in a small box near the back. Editors defend this as routine: corrections are numerous, and giving each one the prominence of the original story would crowd out the news. Yet the practice means that most readers who absorbed the mistake never meet the fix, so the record the paper leaves in its readers' minds stays wrong even after the paper itself has set it right. If a correction is meant to repair the harm an error caused, rather than merely to place the truth somewhere on file, it should reach roughly the audience the error reached. A serious mistake deserves a correction as visible as the story that carried it.
V02-E-003: Audiences who grow up with subtitled foreign films often regard dubbing as a betrayal: the actor's voice, half the performance, is replaced by a stranger's. Audiences raised on dubbing reply that subtitles betray the image instead, since the viewer's eyes spend much of each scene at the bottom of the frame and miss faces, gestures and composition. Each side is right about what the other loses and quiet about what its own method loses. Subtitles preserve the sound of a performance but condense its words, often dropping a good deal of the dialogue to suit the reading speed of viewers; dubbing keeps more of the dialogue and the whole image but sacrifices the voice. Neither is a transparent window onto the original. The choice is between two different losses, and preferring one is a judgement about which part of a film matters most, not a recognition that one method is faithful and the other is not.
V02-E-004: Lists of 'untranslatable' words circulate widely, each entry presented as proof that some culture has grasped a feeling the rest of us cannot even name. The charm of such lists rests on a confusion. That a language has no single word for something does not mean its speakers lack the concept; a phrase of five words can capture what another language packs into one, and the lists themselves translate every entry in a sentence. What is genuinely hard to carry across is different: the associations a word has gathered through use, the contexts where it feels natural, the tone it strikes in a joke or a lament. These are real losses, but they afflict ordinary words as much as exotic ones, and they are a matter of degree rather than an absolute barrier. The lists, by celebrating a handful of curiosities, end up obscuring where the real difficulty of translation lies.
V02-E-005: Research on smaller classes is often summarised as showing that reducing class size raises achievement, and some carefully designed trials do find gains, especially for younger pupils and those from poorer homes. But the finding is easily stretched. The gains appear when classes shrink substantially and when there are enough capable teachers to staff the new classes; a large programme that must hire quickly may fill many rooms with inexperienced teachers and lose much of the benefit. Smaller classes are also expensive, and the same money might buy other things, such as tutoring or better materials. The evidence supports smaller classes as one useful option under the right conditions, not as a reform that reliably pays off wherever it is tried.
V02-E-006: Where the language of the classroom differs from the language of the home, a common policy is to plunge young pupils into the former from their first day, in the belief that early and total immersion produces fluency fastest. The belief mistakes the job of the early grades. Those years are spent acquiring literacy, number sense and the habit of inquiry, and every one of these comes harder when the medium of teaching is itself a puzzle. A pupil labouring over the sounds of unfamiliar words has little attention left for their sense. Beginning in the home language and bringing in the school language gradually need not hold back fluency in it; children who read confidently in one language generally find that the skill transfers to another.
V02-E-007: Supporters of school uniforms often claim that they erase differences of wealth among pupils, since everyone wears the same clothes. The claim is weaker than it sounds. Children are expert readers of status, and when clothing is fixed they turn to whatever is left: shoes, bags, phones, haircuts, the holidays they describe on Monday morning. Uniforms can also be costly in their own right when they must be bought from a single supplier. None of this means uniforms are without value; they may build a sense of belonging or simplify mornings for families. But if they are defended, it should be on such grounds, not on the promise that they make inequality invisible.
V02-E-008: The lecture is now routinely dismissed as a relic: students sit passively while an expert recites what they could read in a book. Much of this criticism is deserved when a lecture is merely a recitation. But it misdescribes the form at its best. A good lecturer does not transmit information so much as demonstrate a way of thinking, showing which questions matter, where the evidence is thin, how an argument can be tested and abandoned. Listeners watch a mind at work in real time, something a textbook, which presents only finished conclusions, cannot easily offer. The case against lectures is therefore really a case against bad lectures, and replacing the form with activities may discard what it does well while curing what it does badly.
V02-E-009: When hospitals introduce short checklists before surgery, asking teams to confirm the patient's identity, the planned procedure and the availability of equipment, complications often fall. It is tempting to conclude that the checklist itself does the work. Yet the same list has produced little benefit in hospitals where it was imposed from above and ticked off by one person while others carried on preparing. Where it helps, it seems to do so by making the team pause together, by giving junior staff a recognised moment to speak up, and by turning silent assumptions into stated ones. The checklist is less a tool that prevents errors than an occasion for the kind of communication that does.
V02-E-010: Patients in drug trials who receive only a dummy pill sometimes report the very side effects listed on the consent form: headaches, nausea, fatigue. This is the nocebo effect, the shadow of the better-known placebo effect. Expecting harm can produce real symptoms, partly because anxious attention makes people notice and interpret ordinary bodily sensations as signs of illness, and partly because worry itself can cause discomfort. The phenomenon puts doctors in an awkward position. They are obliged to warn patients about possible side effects, yet the way the warning is delivered may help bring those effects about. The aim is not to hide risks but to describe them in a way that informs without needlessly alarming.
V02-E-011: Body mass index, a person's weight divided by the square of their height, is often attacked as a crude and misleading measure of health. The attack is fair when the number is applied to individuals without further thought: a muscular athlete can register as overweight, and the measure says nothing about where fat is carried, which matters for risk. But the index was never well suited to judging single bodies. Its strength lies in populations, where it is cheap, consistent and reasonably correlated with outcomes across large groups, making it useful for tracking trends over time. The fault lies less in the measure than in asking it to do a job, the assessment of one patient, for which other information is needed.
V02-E-012: Patients are often told that seeking a second opinion is simply prudent, as if two doctors were always better than one. The benefit is real but depends on independence. A second doctor who reads the first doctor's notes, sees the same scans already labelled, and knows what the referring colleague concluded is likely to anchor on that conclusion, so agreement may reflect deference rather than confirmation. A genuinely independent opinion, formed before the first is known, is more informative precisely because it can disagree. Yet disagreement brings its own burden: the patient must now choose between experts without the knowledge to judge them. A second opinion is valuable less as a reassuring echo than as an independent test, and patients should be ready for it to complicate rather than settle the decision.
V02-E-013: In parks and on campuses one often sees a strip of bare earth cutting across a lawn, worn by walkers who ignored the paved path laid out beside it. Planners sometimes treat these desire paths as vandalism to be fenced off. They are better read as information. Each one records, more honestly than any survey, the routes people actually want to take, usually the shortest line between where they are and where they are going. Some universities have gone so far as to delay paving until they could see where the grass wore away, then laid paths along those lines. A design that people keep walking around is telling its makers something.
V02-E-014: Adding lanes to a jammed motorway looks like the plainest remedy for congestion, yet the relief it brings tends to be short-lived, and a few years on the road is typically as clogged as before. The reason is that congestion had been rationing use of the road. Once journeys speed up, drivers who had been taking other routes switch back, trips postponed to off-peak hours move to the rush hour, some commuters abandon trains for cars, and over a longer span households and employers settle farther apart. The new space is taken up by travel that the jams had been holding down. None of this makes extra capacity worthless, since more people now make journeys they value; it means only that widening is a poor tool for the lasting relief from congestion it is usually sold as delivering.
V02-E-015: Arguments over renaming streets usually set two camps against each other. One holds that a name is a standing honour, and that keeping the name of someone whose deeds a city now condemns means continuing to honour them. The other holds that names are part of the historical record, and that erasing them tidies away an uncomfortable past. Both treat the name as if it had a single fixed meaning. In practice a street name works mostly as an address; few residents know whom their street commemorates, and the honour, if any, is faint. That faintness cuts both ways. It weakens the claim that the old name actively glorifies anyone, but it equally weakens the claim that removing it destroys history, which survives in archives and books rather than on signposts. The dispute is better seen as a contest over what a city chooses to say now than as a battle over the past.
V02-E-016: Benches divided by armrests, ledges studded with metal knobs, and bus shelters with seats too narrow to rest on are usually defended as tidiness: they keep public spaces orderly and discourage people from sleeping in them. The defence describes the intent accurately but not the effect. Such designs do not reduce the number of people who have nowhere to sleep; they move them elsewhere, often to less safe places. Meanwhile they make the city less comfortable for everyone else who needs to sit, including the elderly, the pregnant and the tired. A measure that burdens many people while relocating rather than solving the problem it targets is hard to justify as good design, whatever its tidiness.
V02-E-017: Some moral theories hold that we are always required to do the best act available to us. On such a view there is no room for heroism in the ordinary sense: the person who runs into a burning building to save a stranger has merely done their duty, and anyone who could have done so and did not has done wrong. Most of us find this hard to accept. We think there are acts that are good, even admirable, to do but not wrong to omit, and that praising the rescuer while not blaming the bystander is not a muddle but an accurate reflection of morality's shape. A theory that cannot make room for this category is not more rigorous than common sense; it simply erases a distinction that our practices of praise and blame rely on.
V02-E-018: White lies, such as praising a disappointing gift, are commonly defended as harmless kindnesses: no one is hurt and feelings are spared. The defence overlooks a cost that is spread thin and therefore hard to see. Each white lie slightly lowers the value of the speaker's sincere words, since a friend who always praises cannot be fully believed when the praise is real. Among people who know each other well, the convention is usually understood, and little is lost. But where honest feedback matters, a habit of comfortable falsehood can leave others unable to trust our approval when they most need to. White lies are not grave wrongs, yet calling them costless mistakes a small and diffuse harm for no harm at all.
V02-E-019: Suppose a firm offers work in a poor region at wages far below what it pays elsewhere, and people eagerly accept because the job is better than anything else available. Many would call this exploitation, yet the workers are better off, and had the firm stayed away they would be worse off still. Here a puzzle arises: the firm that exploits seems to act worse than a firm that never came, even though it does more good. The resolution is that wrongness can lie in how a benefit is shared, not only in whether one is conferred. Taking unfair advantage of someone's lack of options can be wrong even when the exchange helps them; but it does not follow that preventing such exchanges is right, since that would remove the benefit without correcting the unfairness.
V02-E-020: A familiar view holds that forgiveness has to be earned: until the wrongdoer apologises, forgiving them merely condones the wrong. This view captures something, since an apology acknowledges the wrong and gives forgiveness something to answer. But it makes the victim's release from resentment hostage to the choices of the person who caused the harm. Someone wronged by a person who has died, vanished or refuses to admit fault would be left with no way to set the injury down. Forgiveness without apology need not deny that a wrong occurred or excuse it; it can mean only that the victim ceases to let the wrong govern their attitude. An apology makes forgiveness fitting, but its absence need not make forgiveness impossible or mistaken.
V02-E-021: When people look back on an unpleasant experience, such as a medical procedure or a long wait, their judgement of how bad it was seems to depend heavily on two moments: the worst point and the final stretch. How long the experience lasted counts for surprisingly little. One consequence is odd but well documented in laboratory settings: tacking a short stretch of gentler discomfort onto the end of an ordeal can make people remember the whole as less unpleasant, even though they suffered more in total. This tells us that remembered experience and lived experience can diverge. It does not settle which one matters more, and a doctor who prolonged a procedure merely to improve its memory would face a real ethical question.
V02-E-022: People asked how long a task will take routinely underestimate, even when they have overrun on similar tasks many times before. The error persists because of how forecasts are made. Planners imagine the particular task in front of them, step by step, and each step looks manageable; the delays that actually ruin schedules, such as illness, interruptions or a supplier's mistake, are individually unlikely and so do not appear in the imagined sequence, even though some such delay almost always occurs. Past overruns are explained away as caused by special circumstances that will not recur. A more reliable forecast begins from the outside, by asking how long similar projects have actually taken, and only then adjusts for what is special about this one.
V02-E-023: Repeated exposure to something, whether a face, a tune or an unfamiliar word, tends to make people like it more, even when they do not consciously remember having encountered it. Familiarity seems to make a thing easier to process, and that ease is felt as a mild pleasure that is credited to the thing itself. The effect has limits, however. It is strongest for things that are neutral or mildly pleasant to begin with; repeated exposure to something disliked can deepen the dislike, and beyond a certain point repetition breeds boredom rather than affection. Familiarity, in short, is a gentle and conditional influence on liking, not a guarantee of it.
V02-E-024: After spilling coffee on a shirt or stumbling over a word in a meeting, people often feel that everyone noticed and will remember. Usually few did. This overestimate, sometimes called the spotlight effect, arises because each of us experiences our own appearance and actions from the inside, vividly and continuously, and we find it hard to adjust for the fact that others are busy with their own concerns. We anchor on our own intense awareness and correct too little. Knowing this will not make embarrassment vanish, but it can make it easier to act without excessive worry about a judgement that, for the most part, is not being made.
V02-E-025: A student who goes out the night before an important exam, or an athlete who skips training before a big race, may seem simply careless. Often something subtler is happening. By creating an obstacle in advance, the person secures an excuse: if they fail, the failure can be blamed on the late night rather than on a lack of ability, and if they succeed despite the handicap, their ability looks all the greater. The strategy protects a fragile sense of competence. Its price is that it makes failure more likely, and it tends to be adopted most by those who are least sure of their ability, the very people who could most use a fair test of it.
